title: Prefix fidelity and KV-cache degradation: regression report for long-context retrievals
body:
Summary:
This regression report documents a focused suite of stress evaluations run during the recent model onboarding cycle. The emphasis is on prefix fidelity (how well a model preserves and uses an early prompt across very long sequences) and observable degradation of KV-cache behavior as context grows (8k, 32k, 128k tokens). We introduce a new set of adversarial prefix tests and cross-boundary retrieval probes designed to expose subtle attention-sink and kv-cache eviction/pathology modes that were not flagged by prior truncation or retrieval tests.

Key findings (short):
- Several model variants show a bounded but measurable decline in prefix fidelity beyond ~24k tokens in synthetic concatenation experiments; retrieval alignment across chunk boundaries is a common failure mode.
- A minority of runs demonstrate transient attention-sink events where a repeated adversarial token pattern causes disproportionate attention mass and KV-cache churn, increasing per-token latency ~18–42% and destabilizing streaming outputs.
- KV-cache eviction heuristics in the serving runtime surfaced an interaction bug with prefix anchoring: early pinned tokens were sometimes evicted in favor of recent retrieval candidates under certain batching shapes.
- Truncation behavior varied by tokenizer boundary alignment — off-by-one token splits at chunk boundaries caused repeated re-fetching of the same retrieval snippet and amplified regression metrics.

Motivation and background:
Long-context and retrieval-enabled serving is a differentiator for our platform. Prior onboarding test suites covered basic truncation and end-to-end recall for retrieval-augmented prompts, but we observed customer reports and internal smoke-test flakiness that suggested more complex failure modes: prefix context decays, retrieval chunk misalignment, and KV-cache eviction leading to non-deterministic outputs under load. This doc records experiments designed to reproduce and classify these modes and produce actionable mitigations for the runtime and prompt design recommendations.

Test matrix and datasets:
- Model variants: three internal checkpoints (v1.6-fast, v1.6-ft, v1.7-quant) and two external open models used as baselines.
- Context lengths: 8k, 32k, 64k*, and 128k tokens. 64k runs were exploratory on private infra only.
- Workloads: (1) synthetic concatenation sequences (synth-prefix-suite) with repeated prompt anchors + injected adversarial repeats, (2) retrieval-augmented dialogue where retrieval chunks overlap tokenization boundaries (retrieval-edge-suite), (3) realistic docs (docs-suite) — multi-section legal and engineering docs concatenated.
- Prompt sets: 120 prompt families covering instruction-following, slot-filling, retrieval grounding, and chain-of-thought traces; each family has 15 seed variations to probe sensitivity.
- Metrics recorded (per-run): prefix retention score (see below), retrieval alignment accuracy (exact-match and fuzzy overlap), attention concentration index (ACI), kv-cache eviction events per 1000 tokens, per-token latency p50/p95, generation divergence rate (BLEU/ROUGE vs baseline), and streaming stability count (partial response resets).

New metric definitions introduced:
- Prefix retention score (PRS): fraction of prompt-specified facts present in the generated completion when the fact was placed at the start of a >N token sequence. Scored via normalized F1 over canonical slot values.
- Attention concentration index (ACI): fraction of total attention mass assigned to top-10 tokens averaged across positions; spikes indicate attention sinks.
- Retrieval boundary jitter (RBJ): number of retrieval chunk overlaps where tokenization splits cause >20% overlap error leading to repeated retrievals.

Experiment design notes:
- All runs use deterministic seeds for sampling where applicable.
- The runtime was instrumented to log KV-cache keycounts and eviction markers; an internal tracer labels pinned/prefix tokens vs retrieval-derived tokens.
- We ran both isolated single-worker experiments and high-concurrency batched experiments (simulating Dedicated pools) to expose batching/eviction interactions.

Results (high-level):
1) Prefix retention (PRS):
- 8k: PRS median > 0.93 across all variants.
- 32k: PRS median drops to 0.79 for v1.6-fast and 0.87 for v1.7-quant; the fine-tuned v1.6-ft remains higher (0.90) likely due to attention distribution tweaks during tuning.
- 128k: notable long-tail — median PRS 0.61 (v1.6-fast) and 0.72 (v1.7-quant); extreme cases dropped <0.40 for adversarial repeat inputs.

Interpretation: degradation is not strictly linear with tokens; adversarially-constructed repeated patterns accelerate drift. The fine-tuned checkpoint shows more robust prefix anchoring.

2) Attention-sink events and ACI:
- ACI baseline at 8k is ~0.12 (expected distribution). Runs that exhibited failures showed ACI spikes up to 0.58 during adversarial windows.
- These spikes correlate strongly with increased latency and an uptick in generation divergence.

3) KV-cache eviction and serving runtime interaction:
- In batched experiments, pinned prefix tokens were observed to be evicted when batch shapes produced uneven KV memory pressure; a race in the eviction policy comparator led to using LRU scores that didn't account for the pinned bit.
- Eviction frequency per 1000 tokens increased ~3x under synthetic adversarial patterns due to repeated identical retrieval keys.

4) Retrieval boundary jitter (RBJ) and tokenization issues:
- Off-by-one token splits were responsible for ~22% of repeated retrieval calls in certain prompt families; tokenizer mismatch between pre-processing and runtime chunking logic was the root cause.

Examples (anecdotal):
- Case A: A legal prompt anchor specifying the client name at token 12 near start; after 36k tokens the model started hallucinating a different name drawn from a retrieval snippet that had an overlapping token window. PRS dropped from 1.0 -> 0.42.
- Case B: Adversarial repeat pattern 'NOTE NOTE NOTE ...' induced an ACI spike and duplicated paragraphs in the output; runtime logs showed repeated insertion of identical KV entries that forced eviction of the prefix anchor.

Risk classification:
- Severity: High for Dedicated/Private customers with strict context retention needs (e.g., contracts, long policy docs). Moderate for hosted API customers using shorter typical contexts.
- Likelihood: Medium to high for workloads that use retrieval with coarse chunking or that intentionally/accidentally contain repeated patterns.

Root causes identified:
- Model-level: attention mass redistribution under repeated tokens; some checkpoints are more resistant (tuned regimens appear to help).
- Runtime-level: eviction comparator bug (does not respect pinned flag under certain batch shapes) and tokenizer/chunker mismatch between offline retrieval pipeline and serving runtime.
- Prompt-level: loosely anchored prompts (early facts placed near token boundaries susceptible to eviction) and retrieval with chunk sizes that cross tokenizer boundaries.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Hotfix to eviction comparator to ensure pinned tokens have higher eviction priority (hotpatch rolled to private infra; PR linked: gh://.../pull/4821).
- Short-term guardrail: if ACI exceeds 0.45 during a stream, throttle batching and force a snapshot of the KV-cache to prevent churn (applied as an experimental flag).
- Tokenizer alignment check added to retrieval preprocessing: strict chunk boundary sanity and overlap checks; if RBJ > threshold then adjust chunk offsets.

Longer-term recommendations:
- Model: add prefix-anchoring fine-tuning objective and adversarial repeat augmentation to the onboarding fine-tune step. This showed ~+0.08 PRS improvement in our small pilot.
- Runtime: implement eviction policies that combine pinned bit, weighted recency, and per-key access rate heuristics; decouple LV cache maintenance from transient retrieval duplicates.
- Prompt engineering: recommend anchor tokens be repeated in multiple early positions and include checksum-like sentinel tokens in retrieval windows to avoid boundary collisions.
- Observability: expose PRS and ACI on per-customer dashboards and add alerting for RBJ spikes.

Action items (owners):
- eng-serv-runtime: finalize eviction comparator fix and add unit tests for pinned eviction (owner: Owen Brooks, ETA: 2025-11-25).
- applied-ml: bake adversarial-repeat fine-tuning into onboarding harness and add PRS monitoring (owner: Maya Solanki, ETA: 2025-12-08).
- data-platform: add chunk boundary verification step to retrieval pipeline and publish a tokenization compatibility test (owner: Rina Patel, ETA: 2025-11-30).
- product: update long-context guidance in the public docs and console tooltips about chunk sizing and anchor repetition (owner: Diego Alvarez, ETA: 2025-12-15).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the expected cost and latency impact for eviction policy changes under extreme throughput for Dedicated pools? Need SRE runbook.
- Should we provide automated prompt-rewriting in the Console for high-risk workloads (e.g., auto-insert sentinel anchors)?
- Is there appetite to add an automated adversarial prefix test as a gate in the model onboarding pipeline?

Appendix: brief methodology details and reproducibility notes
- All experiments, seeds, and instrumentation traces are archived under the linked artifacts. Re-run harness is under gh://redwood-inference/benchmarks/long-context/harness with an automated script run_long_context.sh.
- The synthetics and prompt families are in CSV form with canonical answers in the same repo. Use --tokenizer-version to match runtime.

Conclusion:
This round of regression tests surfaced meaningful failure modes at very long contexts and in retrieval-heavy workloads. Several of the root causes are runtime bugs (eviction comparator, tokenizer/chunker mismatch) that we can fix quickly; others benefit from model-level tuning and new onboarding checks. We recommend shipping the runtime hotfix and retrieval chunker alignment immediately, and scheduling the model fine-tune and onboarding gate for the next release cycle.

Notes to reviewer:
- The body contains experiment logs and example traces in the archived artifacts; please review the PR (linked) for the runtime fix first.
- Feedback requested on whether to add PRS/ACI to the default customer SLA telemetry set.
